passage.text:
Night markets notice
The night markets team needs helpers on Saturday. Bring gloves and arrive before nine.

Message from a friend
I have booked the street food session for Tuesday, but I may arrive late. Please start without me and save a place.

Information sign
Visitors to the night markets may use the tools, but they must return them before leaving.

Short announcement
The visitors meeting has moved from Room 2 to Room 4 because the first room is being painted.

Notice for members
Members can borrow one street food guide for a week. Ask at the desk if you need another copy.

passage.text: The people below want to choose from night markets. Decide which option is most suitable.

passage.label: A
passage.text: Cooking demo tent — An open tent where chefs from three local restaurants cook a single dish twice each evening, so visitors can watch, taste small samples and then copy the recipe at home. The schedule is printed on boards at every entrance, seats are first come first served, and the tent stays open until the market closes.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Midnight food court — A covered food court that opens at nine and serves until the last bus leaves at half past midnight, aimed at workers and students who finish their shifts late. Twelve kitchens rotate their menus weekly, seating is shared and free, and hot meals stay available right through to closing without any time limit on sitting.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Allergy safe stall row — A row of stalls where every dish is clearly labelled for allergies, with dedicated dairy free, gluten free and nut free sections prepared on separate tables. The row was created because many visitors could not eat at ordinary markets, and the organisers check the labels with each seller before the gates open.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Family play and eat zone — A safe zone for families with children under ten, combining a low playground, a buggy parking area and stalls selling small portions that are easy to hold. The zone closes an hour earlier than the rest of the market, and a loud speaker announces the last ten minutes so parents can leave calmly.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Riverside craft stalls — Wooden stalls lined along the river path, where local makers sell pottery, candles, printed scarves and jewellery lit by warm lamps. The setting is quieter than the main square, there are benches between the stalls, and a footbridge at the far end leads directly to the car park and the night bus stop.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Music stage with seating — A small stage beside the food stalls where local bands play short acoustic sets all evening, with benches and standing space that are free to everyone. The music finishes at ten so it never disturbs nearby residents, and the programme is fixed so visitors can plan when to sit down and listen.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Sell your own craft table — A programme that gives beginners a free table on two evenings to try selling their own handmade goods, with mentors on hand to help with prices and signs. Tables must be booked two weeks ahead, and successful sellers are invited to return with a regular pitch the following month.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Covered arcade backup — A glass arcade that hosts the same stalls indoors whenever rain is forecast, so a visit is never ruined by bad weather. The arcade has its own lights and sockets, a notice at the main gate says which sellers have moved, and the covered opening times match the outdoor market exactly.

questions.prompt: Iris collects handmade pottery and printed scarves, and she finds the noisy main square stressful. She wants to browse at a quiet spot beside the water, with somewhere to sit and an easy route back to her car after the market.

Callum has a serious nut allergy and usually avoids food markets altogether. He wants a night out where he can try hot street food safely, with clear labelling and dishes that are prepared away from nuts, so he can relax while he eats.

Paula knits small toys in the evenings and dreams of selling them, but she has never had a table at any market. She wants a few evenings to test her prices with guidance, and hopes to earn a regular pitch if her goods do well.

Nico is a hospital porter who finishes work at ten, hungry and tired. He wants somewhere open after his shift where he can sit freely with colleagues, choose a hot meal without worrying about a closing time, and still catch the last bus home.

Mrs Goma comes with her five-year-old twins and wants them to be safe near the stalls. She needs a fenced play area, a place to leave the buggy, food that little hands can manage, and a chance to leave before the evening gets too crowded.

passage.text: When the visitors in our town started a night markets project, few residents expected it to grow so quickly. At first, the organisers met in a small room and planned one simple activity involving street food. They soon discovered that people were more willing to join when they could see a clear benefit for the neighbourhood. The organisers therefore published a short timetable and invited local businesses to offer practical help.

The project was not completely easy. Some volunteers were worried that the work would take too much time, while others wanted to change the plan every week. The team solved this by giving each person one small responsibility and reviewing the results together. This made the project feel manageable, and it also meant that new volunteers could contribute without special experience.

Looking back, the organiser says the most important lesson was not the final result but the way people learned to cooperate. The group still has problems, especially when the weather affects outdoor work, yet members now discuss solutions rather than blaming one another. For this reason, the project has become a useful example of how a modest local idea can create lasting connections.

parts.passageTitle: Part 4 – Setting Up a Night Market

passage.text: The night market organisers began with a short meeting about evening stalls. (16) The organisers listed foods and local crafts that visitors had requested. The council chose the square because buses stopped nearby and residents could walk there after work. Sellers were asked to label ingredients clearly for visitors with allergies. The choice also gave small businesses a fair chance to meet customers who rarely visited the daytime shops. They wanted visitors to find food and crafts without blocking the narrow square. (17) A simple map showed traders where to set up and visitors where to wait. Before opening, electricians fixed warm lamps above the stalls while organisers placed bins beside the food area. This made the narrow entrance brighter and less crowded. Organisers checked every cable and kept emergency access open behind the busiest row of stalls. The team marked spaces for sellers and left a clear route towards the bus stop. (18) Volunteers checked the lighting before the first customers arrived. Several traders shared storage space, and a local craft maker demonstrated simple weaving beside the entrance. A small band played briefly, but the stalls remained the main attraction. The craft display gave visitors a quieter reason to stay while cooks served dishes from several neighbourhoods. When rain was forecast, they tested lights and covered the most exposed tables. (19) The weather test gave sellers time to protect their goods. A sudden shower tested the plan: umbrellas covered the bread and pottery, while volunteers directed visitors towards the covered arcade and checked the last bus time. The transport check mattered because the final buses were less frequent after the market became busy. The first evening was busy, but the new layout helped people move safely. (20) The market now closes at a fixed time so nearby residents can sleep. The closing routine made the evening easier for everyone nearby. Afterwards, organisers counted visitors and asked nearby residents for comments. They decided to add another bus notice, shorten the queue beside the soup stall and keep the lights on until closing.

passage.text: The market opens (21) ........ sunset, when the square becomes cooler. Sellers arrange their tables and check that each light is (22) ........ working before visitors arrive. The organisers keep a walkway clear (23) ........ people can reach the bus stop safely through the crowd. If rain begins, traders move delicate goods (24) ........ the covered arcade where canvas sheets provide extra shelter. Families often return (25) ........ the food stalls offer small portions and local recipes that appeal to different tastes. The market has become a lively place to meet (26) ........ neighbours and share stories over a warm meal. The organisers weigh leftover food after the stalls close at night. Sellers donate safe portions to a shelter instead of throwing them away. Visitors are encouraged to carry reusable bags when they come to shop. Signs explain where each waste item should go after use. These small changes reduce the amount of rubbish collected after midnight each week. They help traders compare which dishes sell best, so next month they can prepare more accurately. The organisers also publish the timetable online and at the station, which helps visitors choose a suitable arrival time. Traders can then estimate demand more carefully for each evening of the week.
